sections.heading: Effort and the prospect of an extraordinary outcome
sections.content: He connects the ideas through effort: extraordinary outcomes demand extraordinary efforts. answer.summary: MacInnis says extraordinary company outcomes follow a power law, so leaders must keep pushing beyond merely good results; meanwhile, entropy steadily pulls organizations toward disorder. A leader’s job is to supply and preserve the intensity needed to resist that decay.

sections.heading: Power laws make the top end disproportionately valuable
sections.content: MacInnis describes power-law distributions as common across the world and says business outcomes are not linear: reaching 80 or 90% may barely move the reward, while people in the top 10% or 5% can receive 10× or 100× the reward. For company-building, that means aiming for extraordinary outcomes requires reaching the far end of the distribution, not settling for a respectable result. He frames extraordinary effort as necessary for a 99th-percentile outcome, though not sufficient by itself.

sections.heading: Leadership supplies energy against entropy
sections.content: He explains entropy as the tendency of things to move toward disorder: left alone, systems decay. In a company, he says intensity can drop at each management layer beneath the founder-CEO. Leaders should not buffer people from the CEO’s intensity; they should mirror and preserve it, demanding 99th-percentile energy when work reaches the “bored and tired” zone. Otherwise, entropy creeps in and the organization drifts away from the extreme right end of the power law. This is an ongoing effort, not a guarantee of extraordinary results.
